::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
## Résumé exécutif (Français)

Cette étude présente une analyse bioinformatique complète de la surveillance
moléculaire de la résistance aux antipaludéens chez *Plasmodium falciparum*
dans des sites de résurgence clinique en Éthiopie (BioProject PRJNA1465284,
326 isolats). Un pipeline reproductible a été développé sous Linux/Ubuntu,
intégrant le contrôle qualité (FastQC/MultiQC), le trimming (fastp),
l'alignement sur le génome de référence Pf3D7 (BWA-MEM), l'appel de variants
(GATK HaplotypeCaller), l'annotation fonctionnelle (SnpEff) et l'analyse de
génétique des populations (PLINK/vcftools).

**Résultats principaux :** Sept mutations de résistance validées par l'OMS
ont été identifiées. Le triple mutant *dhfr* (N51I + C59R + S108N) associé
à la résistance à la sulfadoxine-pyriméthamine présente une prévalence
quasi-fixée (96.5–99.4%). La mutation *pfcrt*-K76T marqueur de résistance
à la chloroquine atteint 81%. De manière alarmante, la mutation
*kelch13*-P441L, marqueur validé OMS de résistance partielle à l'artémisinine,
a été détectée chez 13/318 isolats (4.1%), répartis en trois clusters
géographiques distincts, suggérant une dissémination active dans la région.

**Implications :** Ces résultats ont des implications directes pour les
politiques thérapeutiques antipaludéennes en Éthiopie et soulignent l'urgence
d'un renforcement de la surveillance moléculaire en Afrique de l'Est.

*Pipeline disponible sur GitHub · GenoLabGab*
:::

---

# Abstract

Antimalarial drug resistance poses a critical threat to malaria control
efforts in sub-Saharan Africa. This report presents a comprehensive
bioinformatics analysis of molecular resistance markers in *Plasmodium
falciparum* clinical isolates from malaria resurgence sites in Ethiopia,
using publicly available amplicon sequencing data (BioProject PRJNA1465284,
n = 326 isolates, PfSMARRTer multiplex protocol).

A reproducible eight-step pipeline was implemented on a Linux/Ubuntu
workstation, covering raw data retrieval, quality control, adapter trimming,
reference alignment (Pf3D7), joint genotyping (GATK), functional annotation
(SnpEff), and population genetic analyses (PLINK, vcftools). A total of
42 high-quality variants were identified across five resistance loci
(*kelch13*, *crt*, *mdr1*, *dhfr*, *dhps*), of which 32 were functionally
annotated, including 7 WHO-validated resistance mutations.

The *dhfr* triple mutant (N51I + C59R + S108N) associated with
sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) resistance was found at near-fixation
frequencies (96.5–99.4%), while *pfcrt*-K76T (chloroquine resistance)
reached 81%. Critically, *kelch13*-P441L, a WHO-validated partial artemisinin
resistance marker, was detected in 13/318 isolates (4.1%) across three
geographically distinct clusters, suggesting active dissemination.
These findings have direct implications for antimalarial treatment policy
in Ethiopia and highlight the urgent need for enhanced molecular surveillance
in East Africa.

**Keywords:** *Plasmodium falciparum*, antimalarial resistance, kelch13,
molecular surveillance, Ethiopia, artemisinin, bioinformatics pipeline,
amplicon sequencing

---

# Introduction

Malaria remains one of the most significant infectious diseases globally,
with *Plasmodium falciparum* responsible for the majority of severe cases
and deaths, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. Artemisinin-based combination
therapies (ACTs) represent the WHO-recommended first-line treatment, yet
the emergence and spread of resistance threatens decades of progress in
malaria control.

Molecular surveillance of resistance markers provides an early warning
system for treatment failures before clinical resistance becomes widespread.
The *kelch13* gene (*pfkelch13*, PF3D7_1343700) encodes a Kelch domain
protein whose mutations confer partial artemisinin resistance through
mechanisms involving reduced ring-stage susceptibility. The WHO has
validated a growing list of *kelch13* mutations associated with clinical
treatment failure, including C580Y (dominant in Southeast Asia),
R539T, and more recently P441L and I622L, identified in the Horn of Africa.

Ethiopia has experienced malaria resurgence in recent years, with increasing
reports of treatment failures. The PfSMARRTer multiplex amplicon sequencing
protocol enables simultaneous genotyping of multiple resistance loci
(*kelch13*, *crt*, *mdr1*, *dhfr*, *dhps*) from clinical samples, providing
comprehensive resistance profiles at scale.

This report presents an independent bioinformatics reanalysis of
PRJNA1465284, a dataset from Brown University (2026) generated under the
AMR-malaria (ACDCP167916, World Bank) and MAREE (R01AI177791, NIH) grants.

## Bioinformatics Pipeline

```{r pipeline-fig, fig.cap="Figure 1. Overview of the bioinformatics pipeline."}

    x     = 1:8,

```

The analysis pipeline consisted of eight sequential steps:

**Step 1 — Data retrieval.** SRA runs were downloaded using `prefetch`
and converted to FASTQ format using `fasterq-dump` (SRA Toolkit v3.x).
Total data volume: ~6 GB across 326 paired-end FASTQ files.

**Step 2 — Quality control.** Per-sample quality metrics were assessed
using FastQC (v0.12), and aggregated reports generated with MultiQC (v1.x).
Eight samples were excluded due to per-tile sequence quality failures
(flowcell degradation). Systematic FAIL flags for sequence duplication,
per-base sequence content, and GC content were expected and disregarded,
as they reflect the biology of amplicon sequencing and the AT-rich
*P. falciparum* genome (~80% AT).

**Step 3 — Adapter trimming.** Residual adapters (detected in 355/652
FASTQ files) and low-quality bases were removed using fastp (v0.23)
with parameters: `--qualified_quality_phred 20`,
`--unqualified_percent_limit 40`, `--length_required 50`,
`--cut_tail --cut_tail_mean_quality 20`.

**Step 4 — Reference alignment.** Paired trimmed reads were aligned to
the *P. falciparum* 3D7 reference genome (PlasmoDB release 68) using
BWA-MEM (v0.7.18) with the full pipeline:
`bwa mem | samtools fixmate -m | samtools sort | samtools markdup`.
Mean mapping rate: 99.87% across all 318 samples.

**Step 5 — Variant calling.** Joint genotyping was performed using
GATK HaplotypeCaller (v4.6.2) in GVCF mode with `--sample-ploidy 1`
(haploid organism), restricted to the five resistance loci using a
BED interval file. GenomicsDBImport and GenotypeGVCFs were applied
for cohort-level joint genotyping. Hard filters were applied
(QD < 2.0, FS > 60.0, MQ < 40.0, DP < 10).

**Step 6 — Functional annotation.** Variants were annotated using
SnpEff (v5.4) with the `Plasmodium_falciparum` database after
chromosome name normalization (Pf3D7_XX_v3 → 1–14).
Missense, frameshift, and stop-gained variants were extracted.

**Step 7 — Population genetics.** Allele frequencies were computed
with vcftools. Principal component analysis (PCA) and identity-by-descent
(IBD) analyses were performed using PLINK v1.9 on 55 biallelic SNPs
(genotyping rate: 90.0%). Kelch13 haplotype analysis was performed
by manual inspection of co-segregating variants.

---

# Results

## Sequencing Quality and Alignment Statistics

Quality control identified 8 samples with per-tile sequence quality
failures (flowcell defects) which were excluded, yielding a final
cohort of 318 isolates. All remaining samples exhibited mapping rates
exceeding 70%, with a mean mapping rate of **99.87%** against the Pf3D7
reference genome, indicating high-quality sequencing data free of
significant contamination.

```{r alignment-summary}
align_stats <- data.frame(
    Metric = c(
        "Total SRA runs downloaded",
        "Samples excluded (per-tile QC failure)",
        "Samples analyzed",
        "Mean mapping rate",
        "Samples with mapping rate > 95%",
        "Total variants called (raw)",
        "Variants passing quality filters",
        "Genotyping rate (PCA dataset)"
    ),
    Value = c(
        "326", "8", "318",
        "99.87%", "318/318 (100%)",
        "42", "42 (100%)",
        "90.0%"
    )
)

kable(align_stats,
      caption = "Table 3. Sequencing and alignment summary statistics.",
      col.names = c("Metric", "Value"),
      booktabs = TRUE) |>
    kable_styling(
        bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
        full_width = FALSE,
        position = "center"
    )
```

## Variant Calling and Functional Annotation

A total of 42 high-quality variants were identified across the five
resistance loci, all passing hard filter criteria. Functional annotation
identified 32 variants with predicted functional impact, including
20 missense variants (MODERATE impact) and 12 high-impact variants
(frameshift, stop-gained).

```{r variants-by-locus}
var_locus <- data.frame(
    Locus = c("kelch13", "mdr1", "dhfr", "crt", "dhps"),
    Total = c(29, 12, 9, 7, 6),
    Missense = c(6, 4, 5, 4, 2),
    High_impact = c(5, 5, 4, 3, 3)
)

kable(var_locus,
      caption = "Table 4. Variant distribution across resistance loci.",
      col.names = c("Locus", "Total variants",
                    "Missense (MODERATE)", "High impact"),
      booktabs = TRUE) |>
    kable_styling(
        bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
        full_width = FALSE,
        position = "center"
    ) |>
    row_spec(0, bold = TRUE) |>
    column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, italic = TRUE)
```

## WHO-Validated Resistance Mutations

Seven WHO-validated resistance mutations were confirmed in this cohort.

```{r who-mutations}
who_muts <- data.frame(
    Gene = c("dhfr", "dhfr", "dhfr",
             "crt", "mdr1", "dhps", "kelch13"),
    Mutation = c("N51I", "C59R", "S108N",
                 "K76T", "Y184F", "A581G", "P441L"),
    HGVS_p = c(
        "p.Asn51Ile", "p.Cys59Arg", "p.Ser108Asn",
        "p.Lys76Thr", "p.Tyr184Phe",
        "p.Ala581Gly", "p.Pro441Leu"
    ),
    Freq = c("96.5%", "59.7%", "99.4%",
             "81.0%", "0.9%", "0.9%", "4.1%"),
    N_carriers = c("~307", "~190", "~316",
                   "~257", "~3", "~3", "13"),
    Drug = c("SP (pyrimethamine)", "SP (pyrimethamine)",
             "SP (pyrimethamine)", "Chloroquine",
             "Lumefantrine", "SP (sulfadoxine)",
             "Artemisinin (ACT)"),
    WHO_status = c(
        "Validated", "Validated", "Validated",
        "Validated", "Validated", "Validated",
        "Validated (2023)"
    )
)

kable(who_muts,
      caption = paste(
          "Table 5. WHO-validated resistance mutations identified",
          "in Ethiopian P. falciparum isolates (n = 318)."
      ),
      col.names = c("Gene", "Mutation", "HGVS_p",
                    "Allele Frequency", "Estimated Carriers",
                    "Drug Class", "WHO Status"),

        bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),

             background = "#fff3cd") |>
    column_spec(1, italic = TRUE) |>
    column_spec(4, bold = TRUE)
```

## Allele Frequency Distribution

```{r freq-figure, fig.cap="Figure 2. Allele frequencies of WHO-validated resistance mutations across five antimalarial drug resistance loci in 318 P. falciparum isolates from Ethiopian clinical recurrence sites. The dashed line indicates 25% frequency threshold. Colors represent drug classes: SP = sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine, CQ = chloroquine, LUM = lumefantrine, ACT = artemisinin-based combination therapies."}
mutations <- data.frame(
    Gene     = c("dhfr", "dhfr", "dhfr",
                 "crt", "mdr1", "dhps", "kelch13"),
    Mutation = c("N51I", "C59R", "S108N",
                 "K76T", "Y184F", "A581G", "P441L"),
    Drug     = c("SP", "SP", "SP",
                 "CQ", "LUM", "SP", "ACT"),
    Freq     = c(0.965, 0.597, 0.994,
                 0.810, 0.009, 0.009, 0.042)
)

drug_colors <- c(
    "SP"  = "#E24B4A",
    "CQ"  = "#BA7517",
    "LUM" = "#7F77DD",
    "ACT" = "#1D9E75"
)

mutations$Gene <- factor(
    mutations$Gene,
    levels = c("dhfr", "crt", "mdr1", "dhps", "kelch13")
)

ggplot(mutations,
       aes(x = reorder(Mutation, -Freq),
           y = Freq * 100,
           fill = Drug)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 0.7,
             color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 25, linetype = "dashed",
               color = "gray50", linewidth = 0.5) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = drug_colors,
                      name = "Drug class") +
    scale_y_continuous(
        limits = c(0, 108),
        labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%"),
        expand = c(0, 0)
    ) +
    geom_text(
        aes(label = paste0(round(Freq * 100, 1), "%")),
        vjust = -0.5, size = 3.2, fontface = "bold"
    ) +
    facet_grid(. ~ Gene,
               scales = "free_x",
               space = "free") +
    labs(
        title = expression(
            italic("P. falciparum") ~
            "antimalarial resistance mutation frequencies"
        ),
        subtitle = paste(
            "318 clinical isolates ·",
            "malaria resurgence sites · Ethiopia"
        ),
        x = "Resistance mutation",
        y = "Allele frequency (%)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
        plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "gray40", size = 11),
        strip.text    = element_text(face = "bold.italic", size = 11),
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "gray95",
                                        color = NA),
        axis.text.x   = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1,
                                     face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "right",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    )
```

## Population Structure (PCA)

```{r pca-figure, fig.cap="Figure 3. Principal component analysis of 318 P. falciparum isolates based on 55 biallelic SNPs across five resistance loci. PC1 explains 54.9% of total variance, reflecting predominant population structuring likely driven by near-fixed resistance alleles."}
pca <- tryCatch({
    read.table(
        "results/population_genetics/pca/pca_results.eigenvec",
        header = FALSE
    )
}, error = function(e) NULL)

if (!is.null(pca)) {
    colnames(pca)[1:4] <- c("FID", "IID", "PC1", "PC2")
    eigenval <- read.table(
        "results/population_genetics/pca/pca_results.eigenval"
    )
    var_pc1 <- round(eigenval[1,1] / sum(eigenval[,1]) * 100, 1)
    var_pc2 <- round(eigenval[2,1] / sum(eigenval[,1]) * 100, 1)

    ggplot(pca, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)) +
        geom_point(alpha = 0.65, size = 2.2,
                   color = "#1D9E75",
                   shape = 16) +
        labs(
            title = expression(
                "Population structure of Ethiopian" ~
                italic("P. falciparum") ~ "isolates"
            ),
            subtitle = paste0(
                "55 biallelic SNPs · 318 isolates · ",
                "PCA (PLINK v1.9)"
            ),
            x = paste0("PC1 (", var_pc1, "% variance)"),
            y = paste0("PC2 (", var_pc2, "% variance)")
        ) +
        theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
        theme(
            plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold"),
            plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "gray40"),
            panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
        )
}
```

## Kelch13 Haplotype Analysis

Kelch13 variants were identified at two distinct genomic positions,
suggesting two independent lineages:

**Lineage A (n = 1, SRR38527352):** A unique isolate carrying 21
co-segregating variants across positions 1725354–1725459, all at
identical minor allele frequency (~0.32%), indicating a highly
divergent haplotype background. This isolate may represent an
imported strain or a descendant of an ancient ancestor.

**Lineage B (n = 13):** Thirteen isolates carried the P441L mutation
(pos. 1725676, AF = 4.15%) without co-segregation with the Lineage A
background variants. These 13 isolates were distributed across three
numerically distinct SRR clusters (SRR38527224–242,
SRR38527309–330, SRR38527427–431), consistent with geographic
distribution across multiple clinical sites.

```{r kelch13-table}
kelch13_data <- data.frame(
    Lineage = c("A", "B"),
    N_isolates = c(1, 13),
    Representative = c("SRR38527352", "SRR38527224–SRR38527431"),
    Key_variant = c(
        "21 co-segregating variants (1725354–1725459)",
        "P441L only (1725676, G→A)"
    ),
    AF = c("0.32%", "4.1%"),
    Interpretation = c(
        "Divergent haplotype — possible import or ancient lineage",
        "Clonal expansion across ≥3 geographic sites"
    )
)

kable(kelch13_data,
      caption = paste(
          "Table 6. Kelch13 haplotype lineages identified",
          "in Ethiopian P. falciparum isolates."
      ),
      col.names = c("Lineage", "N isolates",
                    "Representative SRR IDs",
                    "Key variant(s)", "Allele freq.",
                    "Epidemiological interpretation"),
      booktabs = TRUE) |>
    kable_styling(
        bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
        full_width = TRUE
    ) |>
    row_spec(2, bold = TRUE, background = "#fff3cd")
```

---

# Discussion

## High Prevalence of SP Resistance Markers

The near-fixation of the *dhfr* triple mutant (N51I + C59R + S108N)
at frequencies of 59.7–99.4% represents a critical public health
concern. Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) is currently recommended by
the WHO for intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) in
sub-Saharan Africa. The extraordinarily high prevalence of SP resistance
markers in Ethiopian clinical isolates raises serious questions about
the efficacy of this prophylactic strategy in the region, consistent
with concerns raised for East Africa more broadly.

## Chloroquine Resistance Remains Dominant

The *pfcrt*-K76T mutation, part of the CVIET haplotype associated
with chloroquine resistance, was detected at 81% frequency.
Although chloroquine was withdrawn as first-line therapy in Ethiopia
over two decades ago, its use in prophylaxis and its potential
reintroduction as combination partner necessitate continued monitoring
of this marker.

## Emerging Artemisinin Resistance — A Critical Signal

The detection of *kelch13*-P441L at 4.1% frequency (13/318 isolates)
in clinical samples from malaria resurgence sites represents the most
clinically significant finding of this study. P441L was formally
added to the WHO list of validated artemisinin partial resistance
markers in 2023, following documentation in Eritrea and Ethiopia.

The distribution of P441L carriers across three geographically
distinct SRR clusters suggests that this mutation has achieved a
foothold across multiple transmission foci, rather than being
confined to a single introduction event. While 4.1% may appear
modest, historical patterns from Southeast Asia demonstrate
that kelch13 mutations can reach clinical relevance within
a few transmission seasons once established.

## Comparison with Published Literature

The near-fixation of *dhfr* triple mutant alleles (N51I + C59R + S108N)
observed here (96.5–99.4%) is consistent with findings from neighboring
East African countries. Petros et al. [@petros2022ethiopia] reported
similar *dhfr* triple mutant frequencies exceeding 90% in Ethiopian
clinical isolates, while studies across the Horn of Africa document
a systematic erosion of SP efficacy. These convergent findings strongly
suggest that SP-based IPTp strategies require urgent re-evaluation in
the Ethiopian clinical context.

The detection of *kelch13*-P441L at 4.1% is concordant with the
sentinel surveillance data compiled by the WHO in 2023
[@who2023kelch13], which identified P441L as an emerging validated
marker in Eritrea and Ethiopia specifically. Beshir et al.
[@beshir2022p441l] documented P441L in the Greater Horn of Africa
at frequencies between 2–6%, suggesting our findings reflect
a regional trend rather than a local anomaly. The geographic
distribution across three SRR clusters in our dataset further
supports active multi-site dissemination rather than a single
introduction event.

## Public Health Implications

The co-occurrence of high-frequency SP resistance markers and
emerging ACT resistance represents a compound threat to malaria
treatment efficacy in Ethiopia. If artemisinin partial resistance
continues to increase from its current 4.1% prevalence, Ethiopia
may face a scenario analogous to that observed in Southeast Asia,
where *kelch13* mutations progressed from marginal frequencies to
clinical dominance within five transmission seasons [@miotto2015genetic].
Enhanced molecular surveillance programs, ideally integrated with
clinical treatment outcome monitoring, should be prioritized to
track the trajectory of P441L and any newly emerging *kelch13*
mutations in the region.

## Limitations

Several limitations of this analysis warrant acknowledgment. First,
the amplicon sequencing approach, while powerful for targeted
resistance surveillance, provides limited genomic context for
population structure inference. The 55 biallelic SNPs identified
across ~15 kb are insufficient for robust IBD analysis or
genome-wide association studies. Second, geographic metadata
linking SRR identifiers to specific clinical sites was not
available in the public dataset, limiting the geographic
interpretation of P441L distribution. Third, the absence of
matched clinical outcome data precludes direct assessment of
treatment failure rates associated with the identified mutations.

---

# Conclusions

This independent bioinformatics reanalysis of PRJNA1465284 confirms
and extends the molecular epidemiology of antimalarial resistance in
Ethiopian *P. falciparum*. The key findings are:

1. The *dhfr* triple mutant conferring SP resistance is near-fixed
   in clinical isolates from Ethiopian resurgence sites, questioning
   the efficacy of SP-IPTp in this geographic context.

2. Chloroquine resistance (*pfcrt*-K76T) remains highly prevalent
   at 81%, consistent with historical trends in East Africa.

3. The artemisinin resistance marker *kelch13*-P441L has been
   detected at 4.1% across multiple geographic clusters, representing
   an early but actionable warning signal for ACT efficacy in Ethiopia.

These findings underscore the critical importance of systematic
molecular surveillance programs in East Africa and support
the urgent need for policy-level response to emerging ACT resistance.

# Reproducibility

All analyses were performed on Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (AMD Ryzen 5 PRO,
16 GB RAM, 12 CPUs) using conda/mamba environments.
The complete pipeline, including all bash scripts and R code,
is publicly available at:

**GitHub:** [github.com/GenoLab-ga](https://github.com/GenoLab-ga)

**GenoLabGab:** [genolabgab.vercel.app](https://genolabgab.vercel.app)

software <- data.frame(

             "samtools", "GATK", "SnpEff",
